instruction: Recursively make every file under build readable and executable by everyone.
context: chmod: -R is the recursive flag; lowercase -r is not a flag at all, it is the mode operand meaning 'remove read permission'. Capital X sets the execute bit only on directories and files that already have one, unlike lowercase x.

instruction: Strip read permission from secrets.env for all users.
context: chmod: -r here is a symbolic mode, not an option; it removes the read bit for user, group, and other. This is why 'chmod -r dir' does not recurse the way people expect. Recursion is -R.

instruction: Search the whole src tree for TODO, following every symbolic link it encounters.
context: grep: -R follows all symbolic links during the walk; -r follows only links named on the command line. Both recurse, so the difference shows up when a subdirectory is a symlink. -n prefixes line numbers.

instruction: Recursively search src for TODO without following symlinked directories.
context: grep: -r recurses but does not follow symbolic links found inside the tree, which avoids infinite loops and duplicate hits. Use -R only when you deliberately want links followed.

instruction: List only the names of files under src that mention 'deprecated'.
context: grep: -l prints the name of each file that has at least one match and stops reading it. Capital -L is the exact opposite, printing files with no match. Mixing these two up silently inverts the result.

instruction: Find Python files under src that are missing a license header.
context: grep: -L prints files containing no match, which is how you audit for something absent. -l would print the files that already comply. --include limits the walk to matching basenames.

instruction: Count how many lines in app.log contain the word ERROR.
context: grep: lowercase -c prints a count of matching lines. Capital -C takes a number and prints that many lines of context around each match, so 'grep -C ERROR' consumes ERROR as the context count and fails.

instruction: Show each ERROR line in app.log with three lines on either side.
context: grep: -C NUM prints NUM lines of leading and trailing context. -B NUM is before-only and -A NUM is after-only. Lowercase -c would instead print a bare count.

instruction: Show every line of config.ini that is not a comment.
context: grep: -v inverts the match and prints non-matching lines. Capital -V prints the grep version and exits, ignoring your pattern entirely, which looks like a silent no-op in a pipeline.

instruction: Find 'warning' in app.log regardless of capitalization.
context: grep: -i ignores case when matching. Capital -I is unrelated: it treats binary files as non-matching, equivalent to --binary-files=without-match.

instruction: Recursively search the whole repository for 'api_key' but skip binary files entirely.
context: grep: -I suppresses binary files instead of printing 'Binary file matches'. -n adds line numbers and -R recurses following symlinks. Lowercase -i would instead mean ignore-case.

instruction: Find the identifier 'id' in src as a whole word, not as part of longer names.
context: grep: -w requires the match to be bounded by non-word characters, so 'uuid' and 'identity' are excluded. -x is stricter still and requires the pattern to match the entire line.

instruction: Sort sizes.txt numerically from largest to smallest.
context: sort: -r reverses the comparison so the sort runs descending, and -n compares numerically. Capital -R is completely different: it shuffles the input into random order.

instruction: Shuffle the lines of hosts.txt into random order.
context: sort: -R sorts by a random hash of the keys, effectively shuffling. Identical lines still group together; use shuf for a true independent shuffle. Lowercase -r would merely reverse the sort.

instruction: Show the largest directories under /var by size with human-readable units.
context: sort: -h understands human-readable suffixes such as K, M, and G, so 2G sorts above 900M. Plain -n would compare the leading digits only and rank 900 above 2. du -s summarizes each argument and -h formats the size.

instruction: Keep one line per user from accounts.tsv, comparing only the second column.
context: sort: -u drops duplicates as judged by the sort key, not the whole line, so -k2,2 makes uniqueness depend on column two alone. Writing -k2 without the end field extends the key to the end of the line.

instruction: List files in the current directory oldest first with details.
context: ls: -t sorts by modification time newest first, and -r reverses that to oldest first. Capital -R is not a reverse flag at all; it recurses into subdirectories.

instruction: List the contents of docs and every directory beneath it.
context: ls: -R walks subdirectories recursively and prints a header per directory. Lowercase -r only reverses the sort order of a single listing.

instruction: Copy the whole config directory to a backup location, preserving timestamps and permissions.
context: cp: -a is archive mode, equivalent to -dR --preserve=all, so it implies recursion and keeps ownership, mode, and timestamps. Plain -r or -R recurses but resets metadata to the copying user.

instruction: Copy every file from staging into public without overwriting anything that already exists.
context: cp: -n is no-clobber and silently skips existing destinations, whereas -i asks interactively and is useless in a script. The trailing /. copies the directory contents rather than nesting staging inside public.

instruction: Delete all the .tmp files here but ask me once before removing a large batch.
context: rm: capital -I prompts a single time when removing more than three files, which is a practical guard against a bad glob. Lowercase -i prompts once per file and trains you to hold down Enter.

instruction: Download the release tarball and save it as release.tar.gz.
context: curl: lowercase -o takes an explicit filename. Capital -O takes no argument and reuses the remote basename. -fsSL is the standard bundle: fail on HTTP errors, silent progress, still show errors, follow redirects.

instruction: Download this file keeping whatever name the server uses.
context: curl: capital -O writes to the remote filename and takes no argument of its own, so it can be bundled into -fsSLO. Lowercase -o would swallow the URL as its filename argument and then have nothing to fetch.

instruction: Check the response headers for a URL without downloading the body.
context: curl: capital -I issues a HEAD request and prints only headers. Lowercase -i prints the headers followed by the full body. -sS keeps the progress meter quiet while still reporting real errors.

instruction: Fetch a JSON endpoint quietly in a script but fail loudly on an HTTP error.
context: curl: -f makes HTTP status 400 and above a non-zero exit instead of writing an error page to stdout. -s hides the progress meter and -S re-enables the error message that -s would otherwise also hide, which is why they are almost always paired.

instruction: Download a file with wget and save it as data.json.
context: wget: capital -O names the output file, the exact inverse of curl where lowercase -o does that job. wget's lowercase -o redirects the log messages to a file instead, so mixing them up writes your download into a logfile path.

instruction: Connect to build.example.com on port 2222.
context: ssh: lowercase -p selects the port. scp and sftp use capital -P for the same thing, which is one of the most common cross-tool flag mismatches.

instruction: Copy report.csv to the server's tmp directory over port 2222.
context: scp: capital -P is the port, unlike ssh which uses lowercase -p. scp's lowercase -p is unrelated and preserves modification times and modes.

instruction: Forward my local port 5433 to the database port on the remote host.
context: ssh: capital -L sets up local port forwarding as LOCALPORT:HOST:REMOTEPORT. Lowercase -l is the login username instead. -N opens the tunnel without running a remote command.

instruction: Log into the deploy host as the ci user.
context: ssh: lowercase -l gives the remote login name, equivalent to writing ci@deploy.example.com. Capital -L would instead be read as a port-forward specification and reject the hostname.

instruction: Rename every .txt file under docs to .md, one invocation per file.
context: xargs: capital -I defines a replacement token and implies one command per input line. Lowercase -i is a deprecated alias that defaults the token to {}. -print0 and -0 pair up so filenames containing spaces survive the pipe.

instruction: Gzip every log file under /var/log using four processes at once.
context: xargs: capital -P sets the number of parallel processes and -n 1 gives each process a single file. -r suppresses the run when input is empty, which is GNU-only. Lowercase -p would instead prompt interactively before each command.

instruction: Extract release.tar.gz into the build directory.
context: tar: the bundle -xzf reads as extract, gzip, file. -f must come last in the bundle because it consumes the next argument as the archive name. -C changes directory before extracting, so it applies to the destination not the archive path.

instruction: Extract an xz-compressed archive named toolchain.tar.xz.
context: tar: capital -J selects xz compression, lowercase -j selects bzip2, and -z selects gzip. Modern GNU tar can auto-detect with -xaf, but the explicit letter is unambiguous.

instruction: See what is inside release.tar.gz before extracting it.
context: tar: -t lists the table of contents without writing anything to disk. Swapping -t for -x is the difference between inspecting an archive and spraying it across the current directory.

instruction: Create a gzip archive of the dist directory called dist.tar.gz.
context: tar: -c creates, -z pipes through gzip, and -f names the output. The archive name must immediately follow -f, so 'tar -cfz' would try to use z as the filename.

instruction: Mirror the site directory to the web server, showing progress.
context: rsync: lowercase -a is archive mode and implies recursion plus metadata preservation. Capital -A is only ACLs. The trailing slash on site/ copies the contents rather than creating a nested site directory, which is rsync's sharpest edge.

instruction: Preview what a mirroring sync would delete on the destination before running it.
context: rsync: -n is --dry-run and prints the transfer without touching the destination. Pairing it with --delete is the safe way to discover that a missing trailing slash would have wiped the target.

instruction: Show the first 200 bytes of a binary file to inspect its magic number.
context: head: -c counts bytes and -n counts lines. On a binary file -n is nearly meaningless because newlines appear at random offsets.

instruction: Count the characters, not the bytes, in a UTF-8 document.
context: wc: -m counts characters using the current locale, while -c counts bytes. For UTF-8 text containing non-ASCII characters the two numbers differ, and -c is the one that overcounts.

instruction: The disk says it has space but writes are failing; check inode usage.
context: df: -i reports inode counts instead of block usage, which is how a filesystem full of tiny files runs out of capacity while -h still shows free space. -h formats the numbers with unit suffixes.

instruction: Show each distinct error message in app.log with how many times it occurred, most frequent first.
context: uniq: -c prefixes each group with its count, but uniq only collapses adjacent duplicates, so the input must be sorted first. The trailing sort -nr then ranks by the numeric count descending.

instruction: List only the checksums in sums.txt that appear more than once.
context: uniq: -d prints one copy of each duplicated group and nothing for unique lines. -u is the inverse and prints only lines that never repeat. Both require sorted input.

instruction: Show every running process with its full command line.
context: ps: -e selects all processes and -f gives the full-format listing in UNIX style, where options take a leading dash. The BSD style spelling is 'ps aux' with no dash at all; the two syntaxes are separate dialects and cannot be freely mixed.

instruction: Ask process 4821 to shut down cleanly.
context: kill: -TERM is signal 15 and can be caught so the process can flush state and exit. -KILL is signal 9, cannot be caught, and leaves temporary files and locks behind. Try TERM before KILL.

instruction: Point current at the release-42 directory, replacing any existing link.
context: ln: -s makes a symbolic rather than hard link, -f replaces an existing target, and -n treats an existing symlink-to-directory as a file so the link is replaced instead of created inside it. Omitting -n is why repeated deploys nest links.

instruction: Compare two config files as a unified diff, ignoring whitespace changes.
context: diff: lowercase -w ignores all whitespace when comparing lines. Capital -W sets the output column width for side-by-side mode and expects a number, so it will consume your filename.

instruction: Find README files under the project regardless of how they are capitalized.
context: find: -iname is the case-insensitive form of -name. The pattern must be quoted so the shell passes the asterisk to find instead of expanding it against the current directory first.

instruction: List directories exactly one level below the current directory.
context: find: -maxdepth and -mindepth are global options and GNU find warns if they appear after a test. -mindepth 1 excludes the starting directory itself, which -maxdepth 1 alone would still print.

instruction: Extract a gzip archive into the build directory on macOS.
context: tar: macOS ships bsdtar built on libarchive, but the -x, -z, -f, and -C bundle is spelled identically to GNU tar. bsdtar also auto-detects compression, so -xf alone would work here.

instruction: Recursively list the docs directory on macOS with human-readable sizes.
context: ls: BSD ls on macOS keeps the same -R for recursive and -r for reverse split as GNU. -h attaches unit suffixes to the sizes shown by -l.

instruction: Download an installer on macOS and save it under a chosen name.
context: curl: macOS ships curl in the base system and the -o versus -O distinction is identical to Linux. Lowercase -o names the file; capital -O reuses the remote basename.

instruction: Copy a file from a Mac to a server listening on port 2222.
context: scp: capital -P is the port on macOS as on Linux, still the inverse of ssh's lowercase -p. macOS bundles the same OpenSSH client, so the mismatch carries over unchanged.
